steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on ArCHer, a hierarchical multi-turn reinforcement learning framework for training LLM agents. Explain why single-turn methods fall short for agent tasks, what makes multi-turn RL hard, and summarize our approach and results.

steps.text:
## Introduction

- LLMs as agents: tasks need multi-turn decisions
- Current methods are myopic (imitation / single-turn preferences)
- Challenges of multi-turn RL for LLMs
- Our hierarchical approach
- Contribution: ArCHer and results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction

- LLMs as agents
  - generalist knowledge -> potential for decision-making / "agent" problems in text
  - writing code, navigating the web, using tools, interacting with humans
  - need sequence of intelligent decisions over multiple turns, not most probable completion per step
- Myopic current methods
  - mimic successful demonstrations per step, or optimize single-turn preferences
  - single-turn: poor credit assignment (miss good actions that look suboptimal now but help long-term)
  - no information-seeking behavior (e.g. new tool)
  - goal: multi-turn RL maximizing long-term objective (e.g. customer satisfaction at end of conversation), scalar reward
- Challenges of multi-turn RL
  - online interaction with humans / web servers: slow, expensive
  - on-policy (PPO) impractical: no data reuse
  - off-policy offline: token-level methods treat tokens as actions -> reward over extremely long horizons (more tokens with more turns, LLM bias to long responses)
  - very slow learning: token-level ILQL > 10 days to converge vs filtered BC < 1 day
  - utterance as action: enormous variable-size action space; TD methods need max over action each step
  - need a "sweet spot"
- Our approach
  - hierarchical RL with LMs addressing both on-policy and off-policy issues
  - high level: off-policy TD learning of utterance-level value function
  - low level: any on-policy policy gradient algorithm for token generation per turn, high-level value as terminal reward
  - sample reuse, faster convergence; no Bellman backups over tokens, no max over huge action spaces; critic at coarser time-scale on actor's tokens
  - inherits implementation details from token-level single-turn RL with preferences
  - best of utterance/token-based and off/on-policy
- Contribution
  - Actor-Critic framework with a Hierarchical Structure (ArCHer)
  - several algorithmic instantiations; language "agent" tasks with active data collection ("online")
  - 100x more sample efficient than on-policy (PPO); better final performance than off-policy
  - easy to build on single-turn RL; scales to different transformer architectures and up to 7 billion scale; plug-and-play

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Because they have generalist knowledge, large language models (LLMs) have a tremendous potential to solve many kinds of decision-making or "agent" problems that can be expressed in text or natural language, such as writing code, navigating the web, using tools, and interacting with humans. To succeed in these domains, an LLM has to make a sequence of intelligent decisions over multiple turns of interaction, instead of just generating the most probable text completion at each step.

Even though these agent problems are multi-turn, most methods for getting goal-directed behavior from LLMs rely on myopic objectives. They either try to mimic successful demonstrations at each step, or they optimize for single-turn preferences. Policies trained with single-turn approaches often do not do effective credit assignment (e.g., they do not identify good actions that may lead to good long-term performance even though they look suboptimal at a given step), and they do not give policies information-seeking behavior, which is important in agent problems (e.g., when dealing with a new tool). So in this paper we consider the problem of building multi-turn RL approaches that can directly maximize the long-term objective of interest (e.g., customer satisfaction at the end of a multi-turn conversation with an LLM assistant), formulated through a scalar reward function.

- Our approach
  - hierarchical RL for LMs, addresses on-policy and off-policy issues
  - high level: off-policy TD learning of utterance-level value function
  - low level: any on-policy policy gradient for tokens in each turn; high-level value = terminal reward
  - sample reuse, faster convergence; no token-level Bellman backups, no max over huge action space; critic on coarser time-scale
  - reuses implementation details of token-level single-turn RL with preferences
- Contribution: ArCHer (Actor-Critic framework with a Hierarchical Structure)
  - several instantiations; language "agent" tasks, online setting
  - 100x more sample efficient than PPO; better than off-policy methods
  - easy to build on single-turn RL; scales across transformer architectures, up to 7 billion; plug-and-play

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Because they have generalist knowledge, large language models (LLMs) have a tremendous potential to solve many kinds of decision-making or "agent" problems that can be expressed in text or natural language, such as writing code, navigating the web, using tools, and interacting with humans. To succeed in these domains, an LLM has to make a sequence of intelligent decisions over multiple turns of interaction, instead of just generating the most probable text completion at each step.

Even though these agent problems are multi-turn, most methods for getting goal-directed behavior from LLMs rely on myopic objectives. They either try to mimic successful demonstrations at each step, or they optimize for single-turn preferences. Policies trained with single-turn approaches often do not do effective credit assignment (e.g., they do not identify good actions that may lead to good long-term performance even though they look suboptimal at a given step), and they do not give policies information-seeking behavior, which is important in agent problems (e.g., when dealing with a new tool). So in this paper we consider the problem of building multi-turn RL approaches that can directly maximize the long-term objective of interest (e.g., customer satisfaction at the end of a multi-turn conversation with an LLM assistant), formulated through a scalar reward function.

Training LLMs with multi-turn RL, unlike single-step RL, has a number of unique challenges. First, multi-turn RL would need online interaction with external sources like humans or web servers, and this can be slow and expensive. Because of this, on-policy methods such as PPO quickly become impractical, since they cannot reuse data from past interaction. Off-policy fully offline methods avoid this problem, but they have other challenges. The number of tokens increases with multiple turns (often by a lot, because LLMs are biased towards producing long responses), so token-level methods that treat individual tokens as actions now have to propagate reward signal over extremely long horizons. This makes learning extremely slow over long horizons for token-level algorithms. For example, in our experiments token-level ILQL takes more than 10 days to converge on a task, while filtered behavior cloning takes less than a day. In principle one can deal with long horizons by treating the entire utterance of each turn as an action, but then there is an enormous, variable-size action space, which is a challenge for off-policy methods based on temporal-difference (TD) learning since they need to maximize over the action at each time step. So we need a multi-turn RL framework that reaches a sweet spot with respect to these challenges.

In this paper we design a framework for building multi-turn RL algorithms that reaches this kind of sweet spot. Our key insight is a hierarchical approach for RL with language models that addresses the challenges of both on-policy and off-policy RL approaches described above. Specifically, at the high level our framework uses an off-policy temporal difference learning method to train an utterance-level value function, and at the low level it uses any on-policy policy gradient algorithm to optimize the token generation at each turn of the interaction, where the high-level value function is treated as the terminal reward for that turn. Unlike on-policy methods, this allows sample reuse and faster convergence. It also avoids Bellman backups over individual tokens and maximization over enormous action spaces, because the high-level critic is trained at a coarser time-scale, on tokens produced by the actor. In addition, for training the policy it directly inherits implementation details from existing token-level RL algorithms developed for single-turn RL with preferences. In this way we get the best of utterance-based and token-based approaches, and of off-policy and on-policy approaches, for training LLMs.

Our main contribution is a framework for developing hierarchical RL approaches for LLMs, which we call Actor-Critic framework with a Hierarchical Structure (or ArCHer for short). We study several concrete algorithmic instantiations derived from the ArCHer framework by running experiments on a range of language "agent" tasks with active data collection (i.e., the "online" setting). We find that algorithms derived from ArCHer are 100x more sample efficient than on-policy methods such as PPO, and they converge to a better performance than off-policy methods. Also, our methods are easy to build on existing single-turn RL methods and they scale to different transformer architectures and more parameters (we show our approach is effective up to the 7 billion scale), which directly allows plug-and-play choices of RL algorithms and models.

## Introduction

Owing to their generalist knowledge, large language models (LLMs) have tremendous potential to address a wide variety of decision-making or "agent" problems that can be expressed in text or natural language, from writing code [1,2,3], navigating the web [4,5], and using tools [6], to interacting with humans [7,8,9]. To succeed in these domains, an LLM needs to make a sequence of intelligent decisions over multiple turns of interaction rather than generating the most probable text completion at each step.

Despite the multi-turn nature of these agent problems, most methods for eliciting goal-directed behavior from LLMs rely on myopic objectives that either attempt to mimic successful demonstrations at each step [10,11], or optimize for single-turn preferences [12,13,14]. Policies trained via single-turn approaches often fail to perform effective credit assignment (e.g., they fail to identify good actions that may lead to long-term future performance despite appearing suboptimal at a given step) and do not give policies information-seeking behavior, which is important in agent problems (e.g., when dealing with a new tool). Therefore, in this paper, we consider the problem of building multi-turn RL approaches that can directly maximize the long-term objective of interest (e.g., customer satisfaction at the end of a multi-turn conversation with an LLM assistant), formulated via a scalar reward function.

Unlike single-step RL [12,13,14], training LLMs via multi-turn RL presents a number of unique challenges. First, multi-turn RL would require online interaction with external sources such as humans or web servers, which can be slow and expensive. As a result, on-policy methods such as PPO [15] quickly become impractical because they cannot reuse data from past interaction. Off-policy fully offline methods circumvent this problem, but present other challenges: since the number of tokens increases with multiple turns (often substantially, due to the bias of LLMs towards producing long responses), token-level methods [16,9] that consider individual tokens as actions now need to propagate reward signal over extremely long horizons. This leads to extremely slow learning over long horizons for token-level algorithms. For example, token-level ILQL [16] takes more than 10 days to converge on a task in our experiments, while filtered behavior cloning takes less than a day. In principle, one can address long horizon issues by treating the entire utterance for each turn as an action [8,17], but this introduces an enormous, variable-size action space, which is a challenge for off-policy methods based on temporal-difference (TD) learning that require maximization over the action at each time step. This calls for a multi-turn RL framework that can attain a sweet spot with respect to these challenges.

In this paper, we devise a framework for building multi-turn RL algorithms that attains this kind of sweet spot. Our key insight is a hierarchical approach for RL with language models that addresses the challenges of both on-policy and off-policy RL approaches outlined above. Specifically, our framework uses an off-policy temporal difference learning method to train an utterance-level value function at the high level, and any on-policy policy gradient algorithm to optimize the token generation at each turn of the interaction at the low level, treating the high-level value function as the terminal reward for that turn. Unlike on-policy methods, this allows for sample reuse and faster convergence, while avoiding Bellman backups over individual tokens or maximization over enormous action spaces, since the high-level critic is trained at a coarser time-scale, on tokens produced by the actor. It also directly inherits implementation details from existing token-level RL algorithms developed for single-turn RL with preferences for training the policy. In this way we obtain the best of both utterance-based and token-based, and off-policy and on-policy approaches for training LLMs.

Our main contribution is a framework for developing hierarchical RL approaches for LLMs, which we call Actor-Critic framework with a Hierarchical Structure (or ArCHer in short). We study several concrete algorithmic instantiations derived from the ArCHer framework through experiments on a range of language "agent" tasks with active data collection (i.e., the "online" setting). We find that algorithms derived from ArCHer are 100x more sample efficient than on-policy methods such as PPO, and converge to better performance than off-policy methods. Moreover, our methods are easy to build on existing single-turn RL methods and scale to different transformer architectures and more parameters (we show the effectiveness of our approach up to the 7 billion scale), directly enabling plug-and-play choices of RL algorithms and models.
